title: The milk offering
hook: Namdev sings of offering a cup of milk and pleading until the Lord drank it (Bhairao, Namdev, ang 1163)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chhipa: Namdev at his printing table, his mind the measuring yard, his tongue the scissors. Your line was a printer's prayer.

Drink this milk. That's the heart of the prayer, said by someone standing before the Lord with a cup of fresh milk and a jug of water, waiting for it to be drunk. And he pleads. Tradition remembers him as a boy. But the pleading isn't a story told about Namdev by someone else. It's a hymn in his own voice, in Raag Bhairao, in the Guru Granth Sahib.
screen: `DRINK THIS MILK.` → `HE WAITS, AND PLEADS.` → `IN NAMDEV'S OWN VOICE.`

segments.voice: The hymn is on Ang 1163. In paraphrase: Namdev milked the brown cow and brought a cup of milk and a jug of water. Drink this milk, Gobind Rai, he says, and my mind will be at peace. If you don't, my father at home will be angry with me. And then, the hymn says, the Lord looked on Namdev, smiled, and drank the milk, and Namdev went home having seen the Lord. Tradition fills in the setting: his father, away for the day, left the boy in charge of the offering. The hymn itself needs no more than the cup. Look at what he doesn't do. He doesn't know a ceremony, or argue about whether God drinks milk. He brings the best thing he has, fresh from the cow, and simply expects it to be received. His worry is a child's worry: I'll be in trouble at home. And it's that plain, stubborn trust the hymn says was answered. Sikhs read a hymn like this in more than one way. Some hear a real wonder. Others hear a picture of what love does to distance: when the heart offers without holding back, the Lord is not far off. The hymn doesn't stop to explain. It just says, he drank the milk. And for offerings now: the Gurus taught that the Lord wants love more than ritual. Namdev's cup is a small offering, milk from the brown cow, and it's the one the hymn remembers.
screen: `THE BROWN COW, THE CUP, THE JUG.` · `DRINK THIS, GOBIND RAI.` · `NO CEREMONY, ONLY TRUST.` · `A WONDER, OR LOVE CLOSING THE DISTANCE.` · then, large: `HE DRANK THE MILK.`

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water, or hold whatever is in reach, a cup of tea, an apple, a flower, and set it down in front of you. Add no words and no ceremony; just offer it, the way the boy set down his cup, and wait in the quiet without needing anything to happen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you set it down.
Gobind Rai. Namdev's name for the Lord in his hymn: drink this milk, he pleaded, and the Lord smiled and drank it.
Your line: he drank the milk. A small cup, given whole. Day seven hundred sixty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Namdev's milk hymn is sung in kirtan as gurbani, and Sikhs often tell it as a story about loving trust, while Sikh practice itself makes no food offerings to images.

options: Some hear a real wonder, some love closing the distance; the hymn just says he drank.
